rows.name: Qur'an
rows.detail: Kafalah's Qur'anic anchor: Yusuf's herald offers a camel-load reward and declares 'I am za'im (guarantor) for it' (12:72); 12:66 has Ya'qub demand a solemn pledge before sending Binyamin; 12:78 shows the brothers pleading substitution of one person for another.
rows.detail_long: 12:72 is the operative verse: 'whoever brings it shall have a camel-load, and I am bound (za'im) by it.' 12:66 supplies the surrounding pledge context (Ya'qub takes a mawthiq — binding covenant — before releasing Binyamin), and 12:78 the substitution plea ('take one of us in his place'). Together the three verses give personal suretyship (kafalah bi'l-nafs and bi'l-mal) its scriptural footing, later formalized by the schools.
rows.internal_ref: saa.pdf p.6; verse texts pullable live from app data/islamic/quran/surah-012.json

rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2295
rows.detail: The Prophet declined to lead the funeral prayer of a man who died in debt until Abu Qatada undertook the debt — then he prayed.
rows.detail_long: Two funerals are brought; for the debtor the Prophet says 'lead the prayer of your friend' and only prays after Abu Qatada declares he will settle the two dinars. The founding case for voluntary guarantee (kafalah) of another's debt — the app itself topic-tags this hadith 'Kafalah'.
rows.internal_ref: Pulled from app file this session (kafalah_source_extract.json).

rows.timeline_year_basis: no app dating block — 610 period fallback
rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2298
rows.detail: 'Whoever among the believers dies in debt, its repayment is on me' — the Prophet as guarantor of last resort once conquests brought wealth.
rows.detail_long: Completes the 2295 story arc: early on the Prophet refused prayer over debtors; after the conquests he declared himself responsible for any believer's unpaid debt — the state assuming the guarantor role. App topic-tag: Kafalah.
rows.internal_ref: Pulled from app file this session (kafalah_source_extract.json).

rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2291
rows.detail: The Israelite loan story: 'Allah is sufficient as a surety (kafil)' — a 1,000-dinar loan made with God named as guarantor and witness, repaid miraculously by sea.
rows.detail_long: A man lends 1,000 dinars accepting Allah alone as kafil and witness; the debtor, unable to find passage, sends the money in a hollowed piece of wood which the sea delivers. Bukhari places it in the Kafalah chapter as the archetype of guarantee made in trust. App dating: 621 CE, high confidence.
rows.internal_ref: Pulled from app file this session (kafalah_source_extract.json).
rows.display_note: Shown at 621 CE; app dating range 621–621 CE, confidence high

rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2290
rows.detail: Personal sureties (kafalah bi'l-nafs) taken for an accused man until his case reached Umar — Companion-era practice of body-surety.
rows.detail_long: Umar's zakat collector Hamza takes personal sureties for an adulterer until the case comes before Umar — Bukhari's chapter evidence that guaranteeing a person's appearance (not just a debt) was practiced law in the earliest community. App dating: 622-625 CE, medium confidence.
rows.internal_ref: Pulled from app file this session (kafalah_source_extract.json).
rows.display_note: Shown at 622 CE; app dating range 622–625 CE, confidence medium

rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2297
rows.detail: Ibn ad-Daghina's protection (jiwar) of Abu Bakr — tribal suretyship of a person's safety, given and later returned.
rows.detail_long: When Abu Bakr set out for Ethiopia, Ibn ad-Daghina, chief of Qara, took him under his declared protection; Bukhari files it under Kafalah as guarantee of person and safety in pre-hijra Mecca. App dating: 622-634 CE, medium confidence.
rows.internal_ref: Pulled from app file this session (kafalah_source_extract.json).
rows.display_note: Shown at 622 CE; app dating range 622–634 CE, confidence medium

rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2287
rows.detail: 'Delay by a wealthy debtor is injustice; if your debt is transferred to a rich debtor, accept it' — the adjacent hawala anchor.
rows.detail_long: The debt-transfer (hawala) command sits in the chapter immediately before Kafalah in Bukhari; jurists treat guarantee and transfer as sibling institutions. App topic-tag: Transferance of a Debt.
rows.internal_ref: Pulled from app file this session (kafalah_source_extract.json).

rows.timeline_year_basis: no app dating block — 610 period fallback
rows.name: Sunan Abi Da'ud 3565
rows.detail: 'Al-za'im gharim' — the guarantor is liable. The legal maxim of kafalah, absent from Bukhari, carried by the Sunan.
rows.detail_long: The Prophet's farewell-sermon phrase 'the borrowed is to be returned, the guarantor is liable, and debt is to be repaid' becomes the black-letter maxim of every later kafalah chapter. App grading: Sahih.
rows.internal_ref: Pulled from app file this session (kafalah_source_extract.json).

rows.name: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 1265
rows.detail: Tirmidhi's parallel of 'al-za'im gharim', delivered in the farewell sermon of 632 CE — app-dated to the year, high confidence.
rows.detail_long: Same maxim as Abu Dawud 3565, independently transmitted; the app dates this narration to 632 CE (farewell sermon) at high confidence — the single best-dated kafalah text.
rows.internal_ref: Pulled from app file this session (kafalah_source_extract.json).
rows.display_note: Shown at 632 CE; app dating range 632–632 CE, confidence high

rows.detail: Ibn Majah's parallel transmission of the guarantor-liability maxim.
rows.detail_long: Third canonical carrier of 'al-za'im gharim'; graded Sahih in the app's file.
rows.internal_ref: Pulled from app file this session (kafalah_source_extract.json).

rows.name: Ibn Abbas (attrib., Tanwir al-Miqbas)
rows.detail: The earliest attributed reading: za'im in 12:72 glossed as 'I guarantee a camel-load for him' — spoken by the youth Yusuf sent.
rows.detail_long: Tanwir al-Miqbas (in the app) renders the verse: 'he who brings it shall have a camel load, and I am answerable for it — I guarantee a camel load for him.' The companion-attributed gloss that makes za'im = guarantor, the seed of the whole kafalah lineage. Attribution of this tafsir to Ibn Abbas is traditional, not critical — hence the work is 'attrib.'
rows.evidence_display: Tanwir al-Miqbas (attrib. Ibn Abbas), on Q12:72 (text in app)
rows.internal_ref: Passage read verbatim this session from app file en-tafsir-ibn-abbas/surah-012.json (kafalah_source_extract.json)

rows.name: al-Tabari
rows.detail: Al-Tabari collects the chains: Ibn Abbas, Sa'id b. Jubayr, Qatada and al-Dahhak all gloss za'im as kafil (guarantor); Mujahid alone reads it as 'the herald'.
rows.detail_long: In the app's Tabari file on 12:72 he marshals numbered isnads (19543-19551): via Mu'awiya from Ibn Abbas — 'wa-ana bihi za'im, ya'ni: kafil'; likewise Sa'id b. Jubayr, Qatada (twice) and al-Dahhak, against Mujahid's minority reading of za'im as the announcer. He also surveys the qira'at of suwa' and what the king's vessel was. This is the moment the guarantor reading becomes the recorded majority position.
rows.evidence_display: Jami' al-Bayan (Tafsir al-Tabari), on Q12:72 (text in app)
rows.internal_ref: Passage read verbatim this session from app file ar-tafsir-al-tabari/surah-012.json — za'im=kafil chains sighted at reports 19543-19551

rows.name: al-Qurtubi
rows.detail: Al-Qurtubi turns the verse into fiqh: seven masa'il, equating za'im = kafil = hamil = damin = qabil, and testing whether guaranteeing an unknown amount is valid.
rows.detail_long: In the app's Qurtubi file on 12:72 he opens seven legal questions: the synonymy 'al-za'im wa'l-kafil wa'l-hamil wa'l-damin wa'l-qabil sawa'' (guarantor terms are equivalents); whether daman of a majhul (unknown quantity — a camel-load) can bind, answered because the load was a known measure; and the verse as proof for ju'alah (reward contracts), citing al-Shafi'i's positions. The bridge from exegesis to contract law.
rows.evidence_display: al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an, on Q12:72 (text in app)
rows.internal_ref: Passage read verbatim this session from app file ar-tafsir-al-qurtubi/surah-012.json — the seven-masa'il section sighted

rows.name: Ibn Kathir
rows.detail: Ibn Kathir narrates the bowl episode and reads 'wa-ana bihi za'im' as assurance of delivery of the promised reward.
rows.detail_long: In the app's Ibn Kathir file on 12:72 he relates the placing of the bowl in Binyamin's bag (with Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd on what the vessel was) and closes: 'and I will be bound by it — as assurance of delivery of the reward.' The consolidating late-classical transmission, available in the app in AR/EN/UR/BN.
rows.evidence_display: Tafsir Ibn Kathir, on Q12:72 (text in app)
rows.internal_ref: Passage read verbatim this session from app file en-tafisr-ibn-kathir/surah-012.json

rows.name: Mufti Muhammad Shafi Usmani
rows.detail: The modern tafsir layer: Shafi Usmani works through the juristic problems of 12:72 — how a prophet could stage the accusation, and the verse's use for surety and reward contracts.
rows.detail_long: In the app's Ma'ariful Quran on 12:72 he translates za'im as 'I stand a surety for it', then interrogates the episode's legal ethics (the staged theft charge, Benyamin's consent, al-Qurtubi's account) — a 20th-century Hanafi-Deobandi jurist reading the kafalah verse with classical tools. His son Taqi Usmani (S001 in the finance scholars file) carries the same school into AAOIFI. Finance-local figure; chronology from the app's own TK_TAFSIRS (maariful = 1976).
rows.evidence_display: Ma'ariful Quran, on Q12:72 (text in app)
rows.internal_ref: Passage read verbatim this session from app file en-tafsir-maarif-ul-quran/surah-012.json

rows.timeline_year_basis: death year 587 AH / 1191 CE, standard references (finance-local figure; public source)
rows.name: al-Kasani
rows.detail: Al-Kasani systematizes kafalah in Bada'i al-Sana'i: guarantee of the person and of property, pillars, and conditions, for the Hanafi school.
rows.detail_long: Bada'i al-Sana'i's Kitab al-Kafalah gives the Hanafi architecture: kafalah bi'l-nafs (surety for a person's appearance) versus kafalah bi'l-mal (surety for property/debt), the pillar being offer-and-acceptance, with the creditor's right running against guarantor and principal together. Finance-local figure (not among the app's 2,000 core figures — expected, not a gap). Death year 1191 CE from standard references.
rows.internal_ref: saa.pdf p.6; app absence confirmed in _app_inventory.json gaps

rows.name: Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi
rows.detail: Ibn Qudama's al-Mughni (5:71) sets out kafalah for the Hanbalis: guarantee of person and of property, valid across the schools.
rows.detail_long: Al-Mughni's treatment (vol. 5, p.71 in the standard print) records the two types — daman al-mal and kafalah bi'l-nafs — their conditions, and the near-consensus of the four schools on validity, citing the Abu Qatada hadith and 'al-za'im gharim' as proofs. The app holds the work as F0749-B50 (archive.org copy linked) — a READ pill is possible.
rows.internal_ref: saa.pdf p.6; figure + book confirmed in app (core.json F0749, books.json F0749-B50)

rows.name: OIC Fiqh Academy
rows.detail: OIC Fiqh Academy, 2nd Session (Jeddah, Dec 1985): no fee may be charged on an uncovered guarantee — the ruling behind today's kafalah-fee dispute.
rows.detail_long: The Academy resolved that a guarantee (kafalah/daman) is a gratuitous contract of the tabarru' family: charging a fee for bearing another's risk is impermissible where the guarantor has no covering funds, since the fee would be compensation for pure liability — economically riba-like. Modern letters of guarantee and bank kafalah fees are structured around (and disputed under) this ruling.
rows.evidence_display: OIC Fiqh Academy, 2nd Session Resolution (Jeddah, Dec 1985)
rows.internal_ref: saa.pdf p.6

rows.name: AAOIFI
rows.detail: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 5 (Guarantees) codifies kafalah for the industry: bank guarantees, letters of credit, documentary credits.
rows.detail_long: SS5 standardizes personal and financial guarantees for Islamic financial institutions — permitted structures, the no-fee-for-pure-guarantee rule inherited from the 1985 OIC resolution, and the documentation of letters of guarantee. Year shown as tentative 2002; JOB 2 confirms the exact issue year.
rows.internal_ref: saa.pdf p.6

rows.name: Industry practice
rows.detail: Kafalah underpins trade finance, letters of guarantee and takaful structures; the guarantee-fee question remains the live dispute.
rows.detail_long: Banks issue kafalah-based letters of guarantee and standby credits daily; deposit-insurance and takaful schemes lean on the same contract. The unresolved tension is fees: the classical gratuitous-contract rule (OIC 1985) versus commercial reality, with several national boards allowing cost-based charges — contested, not settled.
rows.evidence_display: Industry practice; national Shari'ah board positions on guarantee fees
rows.internal_ref: saa.pdf p.6
